docs.title: OpenTelemetry Masterclass
docs.text:
Welcome! In this workshop you learn OpenTelemetry (OTel) by doing. It takes 2-3 hours. You need your own laptop.

We start with the basics and move quickly. All code is open source, so you can repeat every lab at home.

docs.title: OpenTelemetry concepts
docs.text:
This page is the reading version of the opening talk. It takes about 15 minutes.

OpenTelemetry (OTel) is an open source standard for making and moving telemetry. Telemetry is data that tells you what your software is doing.

We can see OTel as five ideas:

  1. Generate: software creates telemetry.
  2. Collect and process: telemetry is received, changed, and sent on.
  3. Store and analyse: a backend keeps the data and helps you ask questions.
  4. Standardise: everyone uses the same names for the same things.
  5. Control plane: you manage many collectors from one place.

Here is the big picture. Each idea has its own section below.

flowchart LR
    A["Your app<br/>+ OTel SDK"] -->|OTLP| B["Collector"]
    B -->|OTLP| C["Backend<br/>(Dynatrace)"]
    D["Control plane<br/>(OpAMP)"] -.->|config| B
    S["Semantic conventions<br/>(shared names)"] -.-> A
    S -.-> B

docs.title: The three signals
docs.text:
A signal is a type of telemetry. OTel has three main signals:

Signal What it is Example question Traces The path of one request through your system Why was this request slow? Metrics Numbers measured over time How many errors per minute? Logs Text records of events What happened at 10:42:03?

The signals are linked together. This is one of the key benefits of OTel. A log line carries the trace ID of the request that wrote it. A metric can point to an example trace. Then you can move from "something is wrong" to "this is the exact request".

docs.title: 1. Generate
docs.text:
Your code must produce telemetry first. In OTel, you do this with an SDK (software development kit). The SDK lives inside your application.

There are two ways to use it:

  • Auto instrumentation: a library adds telemetry to common frameworks for you. You do not change your code. (Labs 01 and 02.)
  • Manual instrumentation: you write code to add spans, attributes, and metrics that match your business. (Lab 03.)
flowchart LR
    subgraph App["Your application"]
        Code["Business code"]
        Lib["Framework libraries<br/>(FastAPI, requests)"]
        SDK["OTel SDK"]
        Code --> SDK
        Lib -->|auto instrumentation| SDK
    end
    SDK -->|"OTLP (traces, metrics, logs)"| Out["Collector or backend"]

The SDK sends data with an exporter. The most common exporter uses OTLP.

Not everything needs an SDK. Existing Prometheus metrics and plain log files can also feed into OTel, usually through the collector. (Labs 05 and 06.)

docs.title: 2. Collect and process
docs.text:
The collector is a separate program. It sits between your apps and your backend. It can:

  • Receive data from many sources (OTLP, log files, host metrics, Prometheus).
  • Process data: filter, redact secrets, sample, transform, and batch.
  • Export data to one or more backends. It can route data to different places, or send the same data to several (multi-casting).

This is a pipeline: receivers, then processors, then exporters.

flowchart LR
    R1["Receiver<br/>otlp"] --> P1
    R2["Receiver<br/>filelog"] --> P1
    subgraph Pipeline["Collector pipeline"]
        P1["Processor<br/>filter"] --> P2["Processor<br/>redaction"]
    end
    P2 --> E1["Exporter<br/>otlphttp"]
    P2 --> E2["Exporter<br/>debug"]

Why use a collector instead of sending straight from the app? These are the common reasons:

  • You can change where data goes without changing app code.
  • You can remove sensitive data in one place.
  • You can cut volume and cost before data leaves your network.
  • It can read data from things that cannot run an SDK, like log files. (Labs 05 and 06.)

A collector is also one more component to deploy, secure and operate. Sending straight from the app is simpler, and is a valid choice for small setups.

docs.title: 3. Store and analyse
docs.text:
The backend stores telemetry and lets you search it, chart it, and alert on it. OTel does not include a backend. This is on purpose. You can pick any tool that accepts OTLP.

In this workshop the backend is Dynatrace. It accepts OTLP over HTTP.

flowchart LR
    C["Collector or SDK"] -->|"OTLP over HTTP"| D["Dynatrace"]
    D --> Q["Query"]
    D --> V["Dashboards"]
    D --> L["Alerts"]

Because OTLP is an open standard, you can change backend later without re-instrumenting your code.

docs.title: 4. Standardise
docs.text:
Queries are much easier when names are the same everywhere. If one service writes status, another writes http_code, and a third writes response.status, you cannot write one query for all of them.

Semantic conventions are the shared names. For example:

Meaning Standard name HTTP method http.request.method HTTP status code http.response.status_code URL path url.path Client IP address client.address

Standardisation goes beyond names. OTel also standardises the wire format (OTLP) and context propagation, so every language and tool can understand each other. (Lab 08.)

Weaver is a tool that helps your team define, check, and use these names. (Lab 09.)

flowchart LR
    Reg["Schema<br/>(one definition)"] --> Check["Check"]
    Reg --> Gen["Generate code and docs"]
    Reg --> Live["Live check<br/>running telemetry"]

docs.title: 5. Control plane
docs.text:
One collector is easy to manage. Thousands are not. You need a way to see them, send them new config, and upgrade them.

OpAMP (Open Agent Management Protocol) is the standard for this. Each collector connects to a server. The server can see its status and push new config. (Lab 10.)

flowchart TB
    S["OpAMP server"]
    S <-->|status and config| C1["Collector 1"]
    S <-->|status and config| C2["Collector 2"]
    S <-->|status and config| C3["Collector 3"]

docs.title: Where things sit
docs.text: Part Where it runs Job SDK Inside your app Create telemetry and send it Collector Next to your app, or on its own host Receive, process, export Backend Dynatrace Store and analyse Control plane A central server Manage collectors

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Span One step of work, such as one HTTP request or one database call. It has a name, a start time, a duration, and attributes. Trace A group of spans that belong to one request. It shows the full path through your services. Attribute A key and value on a span, metric, or log. Example: order.id = 42. Signal A type of telemetry: traces, metrics, or logs. SDK The OTel code inside your app. It creates telemetry and sends it out. Instrumentation Code that makes telemetry. It can be automatic (a library) or manual (your own code). Collector A program that receives, processes, and exports telemetry. Receiver / processor / exporter The three parts of a collector pipeline. A receiver takes data in. A processor changes it. An exporter sends it out. Exporter The part that sends telemetry to another place. SDKs and collectors both have exporters. OTLP The OpenTelemetry Protocol. The standard way to send telemetry between SDKs, collectors, and backends. Context propagation Passing the trace ID from one service to the next, in a header, so spans join into one trace. Semantic convention A standard name for an attribute, such as http.request.method. It makes data the same across all services. OpAMP A protocol to manage many collectors from one server.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text: Do this before the workshop. It takes about 10 minutes.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: Tool Version Why Docker, including Compose v2 (docker compose) recent Runs the collector and multi-service labs Python 3.11 or newer All code examples Dynatrace tenant + token optional See your data in Dynatrace

docs.title: Easiest: GitHub Codespaces or a dev container
docs.text:
Everything below (Docker, Python, the virtual environment, dtctl) comes preinstalled, so you can skip to Download the lab images.

  1. Do the Dynatrace step first. You need two tokens:
    • an access token (dt0c01.) with the three ingest scopes listed there, and
    • a platform token (dt0s16.) with storage:logs:read and storage:metrics:read. Create it at Account Management > Platform tokens. dtctl uses it in lab 08.
  2. Open the repo: Or, locally, open the folder in VS Code and run Dev Containers: Reopen in Container (needs Docker Desktop).

  3. In Codespaces you are asked for PARTICIPANT (your name), DT_TENANT, DT_API_TOKEN and DTCTL_PLATFORM_TOKEN. For DT_TENANT enter only the tenant ID, for example abc12345 from https://abc12345.live.dynatrace.com. The setup checks the format, builds the full URLs, writes .env for you and configures dtctl. A value that looks wrong is reported and not saved.

    Made a typo? Open .env and fix it. The labs read it every time. For dtctl, run dtctl config set-credentials lab-token --token <new token>. 4. When the terminal finishes, check the output of the prerequisite check. Re-run it any time: python scripts/check_prereqs.py.

Note

Locally, a dev container does not prompt for these values. Fill in .env as described in step 3 below, and run dtctl auth login.

Prefer to install everything yourself? Continue below.

docs.title: 1. Get the code
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/agardnerIT/otel-masterclass.git
cd otel-masterclass

docs.title: 2. Install the tools
docs.text:
• Docker: https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/. Compose is included with Docker Desktop (Windows and macOS) and Rancher Desktop, so there is nothing extra to install. Only on Linux with plain Docker Engine do you add it: sudo apt install docker-compose-plugin. The older docker-compose command (with a hyphen) does not work for the labs.
  • Python: https://www.python.org/downloads/. The labs use the built-in venv and pip. You do not need any other Python tool.

docs.title: 3. Dynatrace
docs.text:
Get a free trial here

  1. Create an API token: Access Tokens > Generate new token.
  2. Add these scopes:
    • openTelemetryTrace.ingest
    • metrics.ingest
    • logs.ingest

  3. Copy the settings file and fill it in: 

    cp .env.example .env

    DT_ENDPOINT=https://abc12345.live.dynatrace.com
DT_API_TOKEN=dt0c01.xxxx.xxxx

  4. Install dtctl, the Dynatrace command line tool. Lab 08 (Semantic conventions) uses it to run DQL queries. Follow the instructions at https://github.com/dynatrace-oss/dtctl, then log in: 

    dtctl auth login

Warning

Never commit .env. It is already in .gitignore.

docs.title: 4. Python environment
docs.text:
Create one virtual environment for all the labs and install every Python package once. Do this from the repo root:

macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

py -3 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r requirements.txt

running scripts is disabled on this system?

Your PowerShell blocks activation scripts. Allow them for this terminal only. It needs no admin rights:

Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass

If your company blocks that too, skip activation and call the tools directly: .venv\Scripts\python, .venv\Scripts\pip.

Every lab that runs Python on your machine uses this environment. Turn it on in every new terminal by running this from the repo root. After that, python works the same on every OS.

macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
source .venv/bin/activate

.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

docs.title: 5. Check everything
docs.text:
macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
python3 scripts/check_prereqs.py

python scripts\check_prereqs.py

The check tests more than "is it installed". It also tries the things that go wrong on company laptops: whether Docker can really download from Docker Hub, ghcr.io and gcr.io, whether a firewall or proxy blocks PyPI, whether PowerShell will run the activation script, whether the lab ports are free, and whether git changed the line endings. It downloads about 65 MB. Add --quick to skip that download test.

Fix anything marked [FAIL]. A [WARN] is fine, but read it: it usually tells you what will go wrong in a later lab. Run the check before the workshop. If something fails and you cannot fix it (for example, your company blocks Docker downloads), tell the instructor in advance.

docs.title: 6. Download the lab images (at the start of the workshop)
docs.text:
The labs use about 3 GB of Docker images. Do not wait until each lab to download them, especially on conference Wi-Fi. When the workshop starts, open a separate terminal, run this and leave it running while the slides are on. It downloads and builds everything, in lab order:

macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
python3 scripts/pull_images.py

python scripts\pull_images.py

When it prints All images are ready, you are set. If the Wi-Fi drops, or a step fails, run it again. It only fetches what is missing. You need about 6 GB of free disk space.

docs.title: Stuck?
docs.text:
• Docker is installed but not running: start Docker Desktop.
  • No module named venv (Linux): install it, for example sudo apt install python3-venv.
  • Dynatrace returns 401/403: the token is missing a scope. Create a new one.

docs.title: Lab 01: Auto instrumentation
docs.text: Time: 15 minutes

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Get traces from a Python web app with zero code changes. You will run an app that has no OpenTelemetry code, and still see spans.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Auto instrumentation is the fastest way to start. In a few minutes you get HTTP spans, timings, and status codes. It is a good first step for any service. You will also see what it cannot know: your business.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
The lab files are in labs/01-auto-instrumentation/. The app (app.py) is a small FastAPI shop with two routes. It does not import OpenTelemetry. Open it and check.

  1. Go to the lab folder: 
    cd labs/01-auto-instrumentation

  2. Turn on the virtual environment you made in Setup. It is in the repo root, so from this folder:

    macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
    source ../../.venv/bin/activate

    ..\..\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

  3. Check that the packages are installed. Read requirements.txt in the repo root. Among others, it has FastAPI, uvicorn, and two OpenTelemetry packages this lab uses:

    • opentelemetry-distro gives you the opentelemetry-instrument and opentelemetry-bootstrap commands.
    • opentelemetry-exporter-otlp can send data with OTLP.

  4. Install the instrumentation libraries. opentelemetry-bootstrap looks at the packages in your environment and installs a matching instrumentation library for each one it knows (for example, FastAPI): 

    opentelemetry-bootstrap -a install
    To see what it would install without installing, run: 
    opentelemetry-bootstrap -a requirements

  5. Tell OpenTelemetry what to do. You do this with environment variables, not code. Pick one:

    DynatraceConsole (no tenant)

    Copy .env.example to .env in the repo root and fill it in. See Setup. Then load it and set the variables:

    macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
    set -a; source ../../.env; set +a

export OTEL_SERVICE_NAME="shop-lab01"
export OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=otlp
export OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=none
export OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=none
export OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN=http
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=http/protobuf
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT="$DT_ENDPOINT/api/v2/otlp"
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS="Authorization=Api-Token $DT_API_TOKEN"

    Get-Content ..\..\.env | ForEach-Object { if ($_ -match '^\s*([^#=\s][^=]*)=(.*)$') { Set-Item "env:$($Matches[1].Trim())" $Matches[2].Trim().Trim('"') } }

$env:OTEL_SERVICE_NAME = "shop-lab01"
$env:OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER = "otlp"
$env:OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER = "none"
$env:OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER = "none"
$env:OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN = "http"
$env:OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL = "http/protobuf"
$env:OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT = "$env:DT_ENDPOINT/api/v2/otlp"
$env:OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS = "Authorization=Api-Token $env:DT_API_TOKEN"

    Print spans in the terminal:

    macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
    export OTEL_SERVICE_NAME="shop-lab01"
export OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=console
export OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=none
export OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=none
export OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN=http

    $env:OTEL_SERVICE_NAME = "shop-lab01"
$env:OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER = "console"
$env:OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER = "none"
$env:OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER = "none"
$env:OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN = "http"
    Variable Meaning OTEL_SERVICE_NAME The name of your service in the backend OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER console prints spans. otlp sends them with OTLP. OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER, OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER none: this lab only uses traces OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN http gives the stable attribute names OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL http/protobuf is what Dynatrace accepts OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT Where to send data: <your tenant>/api/v2/otlp OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS The token, so Dynatrace accepts the data

  6. Start the app with the agent in front of it. Without opentelemetry-instrument, this is a normal app with no telemetry: 

    opentelemetry-instrument uvicorn app:app --port 8000
    opentelemetry-instrument starts your command. Before your app code runs, it turns on every instrumentation library it finds, and it sets up the SDK from the environment variables.

  7. In a second terminal, send some requests:

    macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
    curl localhost:8000/
curl localhost:8000/products/1
curl localhost:8000/products/99

    Type curl.exe. In PowerShell, plain curl is a different command.

    curl.exe localhost:8000/
curl.exe localhost:8000/products/1
curl.exe localhost:8000/products/99

  8. Look at the spans. In console mode, they print in the first terminal. In Dynatrace, open Distributed Tracing and filter by service shop-lab01.

New terminal?

Environment variables and the virtual environment belong to one terminal. If you open a new one, activate the environment and set the variables from step 5 again:

macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
source ../../.venv/bin/activate

..\..\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

docs.title: Token scopes
docs.text:
For this lab, the Dynatrace API token needs the scope openTelemetryTrace.ingest. The later labs also send metrics and logs, so we ask for all three:

  • openTelemetryTrace.ingest
  • metrics.ingest
  • logs.ingest

Source: Dynatrace OTLP export docs.

docs.title: Expected result
docs.text:
For each request you see one server span named like GET /products/{product_id}. FastAPI also adds small child spans for the ASGI send events.

Here are the important attributes on the server span:

Attribute Example Meaning http.request.method GET The HTTP method url.path /products/1 The path that was called http.route /products/{product_id} The route pattern (low cardinality) http.response.status_code 200 The result client.address 127.0.0.1 Who called user_agent.original curl/8.7.1 The client program

In Dynatrace, the list shows one row per request. Open one to see the server span and its two small http send child spans. Note the 404 row: Dynatrace shows it as Success, because a 4xx is not a server failure.

docs.title: What you got for free
docs.text:
• A span for every HTTP request, with timing.
  • Standard attributes: method, path, route, status, client.
  • Context propagation: if another service calls this one with a traceparent header, the spans join its trace. (Lab 02.)

docs.title: What you did not get
docs.text:
• Anything about your business. Which product? How much did it cost? Which customer?
  • The 404 request has status UNSET, not ERROR. For a server, a 4xx is the client's mistake, so OTel does not mark it as an error.
  • Any detail inside the function. The 50 ms of "work" is just part of the one span.

Lab 03 shows how manual instrumentation adds this.

docs.title: Stuck?
docs.text:
• python: command not found or No module named venv: install Python 3.11 or newer. See Setup.
  • opentelemetry-instrument: command not found: the virtual environment is not on (see Setup). Turn it on: source ../../.venv/bin/activate (macOS / Linux) or ..\..\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 (Windows PowerShell).
  • Port 8000 is busy (for example, mkdocs serve also uses it): stop the other program, or use another port, such as --port 8001. Then use the same port in the curl commands.
  • Nothing in Dynatrace, no errors: wait 30 seconds. Check that DT_ENDPOINT has no /api/... at the end. Step 5 adds /api/v2/otlp.
  • 401 or 403 from Dynatrace: the token is wrong or lacks the openTelemetryTrace.ingest scope.
  • Console output is not showing: the console exporter writes in batches. Wait about 5 seconds after a request.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Remove OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN and run again. The attribute names change (http.method, http.status_code). These are the old names. Standard names are the topic of Lab 08.
  • Send to both console and OTLP. Set OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER to console,otlp (export OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=console,otlp on macOS / Linux, $env:OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER = "console,otlp" on Windows).

docs.title: Lab 02: Auto instrumentation expanded
docs.text: Time: 15 minutes

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: See one distributed trace that crosses two services. A frontend calls a backend, and you read the traceparent header that connects them.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Real systems have many services. A trace is only useful if it follows a request from one service to the next. OpenTelemetry does this with context propagation: the caller puts the trace ID in an HTTP header, and the next service reads it. The instrumentation libraries do this for you.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
The lab files are in labs/02-auto-expanded/. Docker must be running.

  • frontend/app.py: a FastAPI service. GET /order/{id} calls the backend with requests.
  • backend/app.py: a FastAPI service. GET /products/{id} returns a product.

Neither file imports OpenTelemetry. Open them and check.

  1. Go to the lab folder: 
    cd labs/02-auto-expanded
  2. Read frontend/Dockerfile. It installs the packages, runs opentelemetry-bootstrap -a install (as in Lab 01), and starts the app with opentelemetry-instrument. Bootstrap finds FastAPI and requests, so it installs an instrumentation library for each.

  3. Fill in .env in the repo root first. See Setup. Then start both services, and give compose the .env file:

    docker compose --env-file ../../.env up --build

    docker-compose.yaml sets OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=otlp, the endpoint ($DT_ENDPOINT/api/v2/otlp), and the token header. These are the same variables as in Lab 01.

    No Dynatrace tenant? Print spans in the console

    Add the console file. It turns the OTLP exporter into the console exporter. Spans then print in the container logs. You do not need a .env file:

    docker compose -f docker-compose.yaml -f docker-compose.console.yaml up --build

  4. In a second terminal, order a product:

    macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
    curl localhost:9000/order/1

    Type curl.exe. In PowerShell, plain curl is a different command.

    curl.exe localhost:9000/order/1

    You get JSON back. Look at the field traceparent_sent.

  5. Read the logs. The frontend prints frontend sent traceparent: .... The backend prints backend received traceparent: .... They are the same value.

  6. Find the trace. In Dynatrace, open Distributed Tracing and filter by service frontend-lab02. (In console mode, look at the trace_id in every span, in both services.)

docs.title: Read the traceparent
docs.text:
The header looks like this:

00-0d8a645dc4d5dcd1c2dbd31cc171983c-eca2e95684aac18e-03
│  │                                │                └─ flags
│  │                                └─ parent span ID (the frontend's outgoing call)
│  └─ trace ID (the same in every service)
└─ version
Part Meaning version Always 00 today (the W3C Trace Context standard) trace ID 32 hex characters. Every span of the request shares it. parent span ID 16 hex characters. The backend's server span uses this as its parent. flags 01 means "sampled" (keep this trace). The last digits can have other bits set; the sampled bit is the one to look for.

The requests instrumentation adds the header to the outgoing call. The FastAPI instrumentation in the backend reads it and makes its span a child. That is all of context propagation.

docs.title: Agent or code?
docs.text:
In step 3 the agent (opentelemetry-instrument) did all the work. You can also turn the same instrumentation on in code. Look at frontend/app_in_code.py. The important lines are:

FastAPIInstrumentor.instrument_app(app)  # one span for each incoming request
RequestsInstrumentor().instrument()      # one span for each outgoing request

Before that, the file builds the SDK itself: a TracerProvider, a service name, and an exporter. The agent did this for you from the environment variables.

Try it. Stop the stack (Ctrl+C), then run the frontend without the agent:

docker compose --env-file ../../.env \
  -f docker-compose.yaml -f docker-compose.code.yaml up --build

Call the app again. You get the same trace:

macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
curl localhost:9000/order/1

Type curl.exe. In PowerShell, plain curl is a different command.

curl.exe localhost:9000/order/1
Agent (opentelemetry-instrument) In code Code changes None A few lines at startup Control Environment variables only Full: choose which libraries, set options, add hooks Good for Fast start, many services, code you cannot change Services where you need exact control, or later add manual spans (Lab 03) Risk Turns on everything it finds (can be noisy) You must keep the setup code correct

docs.title: Expected result
docs.text:
One trace with spans from two services:

frontend-lab02  GET /order/{product_id}      (server span)
frontend-lab02    GET                         (client span, the call made by requests)
backend-lab02       GET /products/{product_id} (server span)

All of them have the same trace ID. The backend span is a child of the frontend's client span. FastAPI also adds small http send and http receive child spans.

Screenshot placeholder: a Dynatrace trace with frontend-lab02 and backend-lab02 spans.

docs.title: Stuck?
docs.text:
• port is already allocated or Not Found from curl: another program uses port 9000 or 9001 (for example, an old Lab 01 app). Stop it, or change the left number in the ports lines of docker-compose.yaml.
  • curl: connection refused: the containers are still starting. Wait a few seconds.
  • Two separate traces, not one: the traceparent header was lost. Check that the frontend logs show frontend sent traceparent: ... and not None.
  • No spans in console mode: spans are printed in batches. Wait about 5 seconds after a request.
  • required variable DT_ENDPOINT is missing a value: add the env file to the command, and check that .env has both values: 
    docker compose --env-file ../../.env up
  • Nothing in Dynatrace: check DT_ENDPOINT (no /api/... at the end) and the token scopes. See Lab 01.
  • Changed a file but nothing changed: rebuild the image: 
    docker compose up --build

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
Exercise: find an error in a trace.

  1. Call product 13. The backend raises an exception for it:

    macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
    curl -i localhost:9000/order/13

    Type curl.exe. In PowerShell, plain curl is a different command.

    curl.exe -i localhost:9000/order/13

  2. Find this trace. Which span has the error? The backend server span has status ERROR and an exception event. The frontend returns 502.

  3. Call product 99:

    macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
    curl -i localhost:9000/order/99

    Type curl.exe. In PowerShell, plain curl is a different command.

    curl.exe -i localhost:9000/order/99

    This is a 404. Compare it: is any span marked as an error? (Remember Lab 01: a 4xx is not a server error.)

Exercise: add a third hop.

The folder inventory/ is ready. It is a third FastAPI service with GET /stock/{id} on port 8002. It is not in docker-compose.yaml yet. Your job is to wire it in, so the trace has three services.

  1. Add the service to docker-compose.yaml, below backend: 
      inventory:
    build: ./inventory
    environment:
      <<: *otel-env
      OTEL_SERVICE_NAME: inventory-lab02
  2. Tell the backend where it is. In the backend service, add this to environment, and add a depends_on for inventory: 
          INVENTORY_URL: http://inventory:8002
  3. In backend/requirements.txt, add requests==2.32.5. The backend will make an outgoing call, so it needs requests. Bootstrap installs the matching instrumentation for you when the image builds.
  4. In backend/app.py, call the inventory service before return PRODUCTS[product_id]: 
    stock = requests.get(f"{INVENTORY_URL}/stock/{product_id}", timeout=5).json()
return {**PRODUCTS[product_id], "in_stock": stock["in_stock"]}
    You also need these lines at the top of the file: 
    import os
import requests

INVENTORY_URL = os.getenv("INVENTORY_URL", "http://localhost:8002")

  5. Rebuild and start, then call the app: 

    docker compose --env-file ../../.env up --build

    macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
    curl localhost:9000/order/1

    Type curl.exe. In PowerShell, plain curl is a different command.

    curl.exe localhost:9000/order/1

  6. Check the result. The response has in_stock. The logs of all three services show the same trace ID in the traceparent. The parent span ID is different in each, because each hop makes a new client span. In Dynatrace, you see inventory-lab02 as a third service in the trace.

docs.title: Lab 03: Manual instrumentation
docs.text: Time: 25 minutes

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Add your own spans, attributes, events, errors, metrics and correlated logs to the backend. Then compare this with what auto instrumentation gave you for free.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Auto instrumentation knows about HTTP, databases and other libraries. It does not know about your business: an order, its value, a declined payment. Manual instrumentation adds that. It costs effort and needs care, so this lab shows what you gain and what you pay.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
The lab files are in labs/03-manual-instrumentation/. Docker must be running. Stop Lab 02 first, because both labs use ports 9000 and 9001.

  • frontend/: the same frontend as Lab 02. It is auto instrumented. It has a new quantity parameter.
  • starter/backend/app.py: the backend with manual instrumentation. Two TODO markers are for you.
  • solution/backend/app.py: the finished backend.

The agent (opentelemetry-instrument) still sets up the SDK from environment variables. The code only uses the API (trace.get_tracer, metrics.get_meter). That is the normal way to mix auto and manual.

  1. Go to the lab folder and start the starter: 

    cd labs/03-manual-instrumentation
docker compose --env-file ../../.env up --build
    Compared with Lab 02, docker-compose.yaml also turns on metrics and logs (OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=otlp, OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=otlp). It sets OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_TEMPORALITY_PREFERENCE=delta, because Dynatrace wants delta values for counters and histograms.

    No Dynatrace tenant? Print telemetry in the console 

    docker compose -f docker-compose.yaml -f docker-compose.console.yaml up --build
    Metrics print every 5 seconds in this mode.

  2. In a second terminal, send three orders:

    macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
    curl "localhost:9000/order/1?quantity=2"
curl -i "localhost:9000/order/3?quantity=2"
curl -i localhost:9000/order/99

    Type curl.exe. In PowerShell, plain curl is a different command.

    curl.exe "localhost:9000/order/1?quantity=2"
curl.exe -i "localhost:9000/order/3?quantity=2"
curl.exe -i localhost:9000/order/99
    • The first order works: 2 keyboards cost 98.
    • The second is declined: 2 monitors cost 600, and the payment limit is 500. You get a 402.
    • The third returns 404, because the product does not exist.
    • Open starter/backend/app.py and read it. Each feature is marked in the code:
    Feature Code What you see Custom span tracer.start_as_current_span("process_order") A new child span under the FastAPI span Attributes span.set_attribute("order.id", ...) Business data you can filter on Span event span.add_event("stock.checked", ...) A time stamp inside the span Error record_exception(...) and set_status(ERROR) A red span, with the exception details Counter orders_counter.add(1, {...}) shop.orders: how many orders, by product and outcome Histogram order_value_histogram.record(...) shop.order.value: the spread of order values Log correlation logger.info(...) inside the span The log line carries the trace ID and span ID

docs.title: Exercise: add one attribute and one span
docs.text:
In the starter, the order value is not on the span, and the payment call has no span of its own. Fix both.

  1. TODO 1: add the attribute order.value to the process_order span.
  2. TODO 2: put charge_payment(order_value) in its own span charge_payment. Set payment.amount on it. Record the error on this new span.
  3. Restart, and send the same three orders again: 
    docker compose --env-file ../../.env up --build
  4. Stuck? Compare with solution/backend/app.py. You can run it with: 
    docker compose --env-file ../../.env -f docker-compose.yaml -f docker-compose.solution.yaml up --build

docs.title: Expected result
docs.text:
For the declined order, one trace with:

frontend-lab03  GET /order/{product_id}
frontend-lab03    GET                              (client span)
backend-lab03       GET /orders/{product_id}       (server span, 402)
backend-lab03         process_order                (ERROR, order.id, order.value ...)
backend-lab03           charge_payment             (ERROR, exception event)
  • In Dynatrace, open Distributed Tracing, filter by service backend-lab03, and open the process_order span. Look at the attributes and the stock.checked event.
  • Open Notebooks (or Metrics) and search for shop.orders and shop.order.value. Split shop.orders by order.outcome.
  • Open Logs and find order ... declined. Open the trace from the log line (it has the same trace ID).

Screenshot placeholder: the process_order span with attributes, and the shop.orders metric.

A 402 is not a server error

The FastAPI span stays without an error status, because a 4xx is the client's problem (Lab 01). But your span says "payment declined" and is an ERROR. Only your code knows that this matters to the business.

docs.title: Auto or manual?
docs.text:
Auto instrumentation Manual instrumentation Effort Almost none Real work: someone must write and review it Detail HTTP, database, framework level Business level: orders, values, decisions Maintenance Update the library Update your code when the logic changes Risk of noise High: it traces everything it finds Low if you are careful. High if you add a span to every function. Cardinality Controlled by the library You control it, so you can break it PII risk Low, but URLs and queries can leak data Higher: you choose the attribute values (emails, names, card numbers)

Rules of thumb:

  • Auto and manual are both valid, and they can be combined. Auto gives broad coverage quickly. Manual gives full control over what is created. Some teams use only manual instrumentation, for example to keep tight control over volume, naming, cost or PII.
  • Choose based on the questions you need to answer and how much control you need, not on a default order.
  • Every span adds data volume and cost. Teams often reserve spans for "an operation worth seeing on its own", rather than wrapping every function.
  • Put business data on spans (order.id is fine here). Keep metric attributes to a small set of values.

Cardinality

Every different combination of metric attribute values makes a new time series. Look at the counter in the code: it uses product.name and order.outcome. A handful of products and two outcomes is fine. If you used order.id or a user ID, you would create one series for each order or user. This makes metrics slow and expensive. Unbounded values like these are usually placed on spans or logs instead of metric attributes.

docs.title: Stuck?
docs.text:
• port is already allocated: Lab 02 is still running. Stop it from labs/02-auto-expanded: 
    docker compose down
  • No metrics in Dynatrace: the metric export interval is 10 seconds. Wait, then check the token has metrics.ingest. Logs need logs.ingest. See Setup.
  • Metrics are there but histogram is empty or odd: check that OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_TEMPORALITY_PREFERENCE is delta.
  • Logs have no trace ID: the log call must run inside the with tracer.start_as_current_span(...) block.
  • Changed the code but nothing changed: rebuild: 
    docker compose up --build
  • required variable DT_ENDPOINT is missing a value: add the env file to the command: 
    docker compose --env-file ../../.env up --build

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Add a quantity attribute to the shop.orders counter. Is this safe for cardinality? Why or why not?
  • Add a second span event when the payment is declined. What data would help the person who gets paged?
  • Look at the traceparent between the two services (Lab 02). Your custom spans did not need any propagation code. Why?

docs.title: Lab 04: OpenTelemetry Injector (discussion)
docs.text: Time: 10 minutes. Discussion only, no lab.

docs.title: 1. Goal
docs.text: Understand what the OpenTelemetry Injector is, how it adds instrumentation without code changes, and where it fits next to the approaches from Labs 01 to 03.

docs.title: 2. Why it matters
docs.text:
In Labs 01 and 02 you started the app with opentelemetry-instrument. That still means you change how each app starts. On a host with 200 services, this is a lot of work.

The OpenTelemetry Injector solves this. You install it once on a host, and it switches on auto instrumentation for the processes on that host. You do not edit each service's start command.

The injector does not collect any telemetry itself. It only helps the OTel auto instrumentation agent for each runtime (for example the Java agent) load into your processes. You still need those agents.

If you know the Dynatrace OneAgent, the "install once per host" idea is the same. Put together, the pieces form an open source alternative:

  • the injector gets the agents loaded,
  • the OTel agents for each runtime create the telemetry,
  • the collector receives it and sends it to your backend.

This is a viable approach, but it is early. It is not a drop-in OneAgent. You assemble and maintain the parts yourself, and the injector is still 0.x. It supports Linux only, and Python is off by default. The OneAgent also comes with vendor support, which this setup does not. See section 5 for the full list of limits.

docs.title: 3. How it works
docs.text:
The injector is a small shared library (libotelinject.so), written in Zig. It does not instrument your code. It only sets environment variables, so that the real OTel agent for your runtime loads.

  1. A Linux process starts. The dynamic linker loads the injector first, because of LD_PRELOAD or /etc/ld.so.preload.
  2. The injector finds the process's C library (glibc or musl).
  3. It uses the library to read and write the process environment.
  4. It adds variables such as JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, NODE_OPTIONS, RUBYOPT or CORECLR_PROFILER. These point to the auto instrumentation agent for that runtime.
  5. The app starts. The runtime sees these variables and loads the agent. The agent sends OTLP to your collector.

If any step fails, the injector stops and lets the process start as normal.

flowchart LR
    P["/etc/ld.so.preload<br/>or LD_PRELOAD"] --> I["libotelinject.so"]
    I -->|"sets env vars<br/>(JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS,<br/>NODE_OPTIONS, ...)"| R["App process<br/>(Java, Node.js, .NET, ...)"]
    R -->|loads| A["OTel agent<br/>for that runtime"]
    A -->|OTLP| C["Collector"]
    C --> D["Dynatrace"]

Two things to notice:

  • /etc/ld.so.preload affects every process on the host. LD_PRELOAD affects only one process.
  • The injector can also set resource attributes, such as service.name and Kubernetes pod names. It reads them from OTEL_INJECTOR_* variables.

docs.title: 4. What it supports
docs.text:
Checked against the upstream README (latest release at the time of writing: v0.11.0, August).

Topic Status Runtimes Java, Node.js, .NET, Ruby. Python is off by default. Operating system Linux only (it relies on ELF and the dynamic linker). C library glibc and musl. If it cannot find the libc, it does not inject. .NET Only .NET 8 or newer by default. It skips apps that already reference OpenTelemetry* packages. Installation DEB and RPM packages come from opentelemetry-packaging. The injector repository only publishes the raw .so. Config file /etc/opentelemetry/injector/injector.conf sets the agent path for each runtime. Filtering include_paths, exclude_paths, include_with_arguments, exclude_with_arguments. Exclusions win. Opt out OTEL_INJECTOR_DISABLED=true for one workload. auto_instrumentation_disabled=* for all.

Python is off by default

The README says it is not always safe to add Python packages to a process, because of possible dependency conflicts. This is why our Python labs use opentelemetry-instrument and a pinned requirements.txt instead.

docs.title: 5. Limits and security notes
docs.text:
Limits

  • Linux only. No Windows, and no macOS.
  • It is young. Releases are still 0.x, and the README gives no stability label. Expect changes. For example, v0.10.0 removed DEB and RPM builds from the repository.
  • It does not create the agents. You must install the agent for each runtime, or use the packages that bundle them.
  • By default it only sets variables that start with OTEL_. Other prefixes need a custom build.
  • For .NET it overwrites existing profiler variables. .NET does not support two agents.
  • Auto instrumentation gives you framework spans only. It does not know your business logic. Business-level spans need manual instrumentation, as in Lab 03.

Security

  • Turning it on for the whole host needs root.
  • A preloaded library runs inside every process, with that process's permissions. It carries the same risks as any code that runs on production hosts.
  • Raw library releases are signed with Sigstore Cosign. The README says to verify the signature before loading the file: "If verification fails, do not load the artifact."
  • A bug in the injector can affect the host process. Release v0.10.1 fixed a crash on older glibc. Many teams test on a staging host first.
  • Injected agents change what data leaves the host. Check which attributes they capture.

docs.title: 6. Discussion questions
docs.text:
1. You have 200 Java services on VMs. What are the pros and cons of the injector compared with adding -javaagent to each start script?
  2. /etc/ld.so.preload affects every process. When would you rather use LD_PRELOAD for one service?
  3. The injector is 0.x. What would you need to see before you use it in production? (Think: tests, signing, release process, who maintains it.)
  4. Your team runs Python services. The injector leaves Python off by default. What would you do instead?
  5. How is this different from the Dynatrace OneAgent? Think about scope, support, and what happens when something breaks.
  6. In Kubernetes, you could use the OpenTelemetry Operator to inject agents. When would a host-level injector still be useful?

docs.title: 7. Going further
docs.text:
• OpenTelemetry Injector on GitHub
  • OpenTelemetry packaging (DEB and RPM)
  • Read the README sections "Design" and "Configuration" to see every setting.

docs.title: Lab 05: Collector basics
docs.text: Time: 20 minutes

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Run an OpenTelemetry Collector that reads a log file and sends the lines to Dynatrace. Then send the telemetry of your Lab 03 app through the same collector.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: So far, every app sent data straight to Dynatrace. That works for a lab. Many setups put one component between the apps and the backend. The collector is that component. It can read files, receive data from apps, change data, and send it to one or more backends. Your apps do not need to change when the backend changes.

docs.title: How a collector works
docs.text:
A collector is a set of pipelines. Each pipeline handles one signal (logs, metrics or traces) and has three kinds of parts:

flowchart LR
    subgraph pipeline [Pipeline: logs]
        direction LR
        R[Receiver<br/>file_log] --> P[Processors<br/>none in this lab] --> E[Exporters<br/>otlp_http + debug]
    end
    F[(live.log)] --> R
    E --> DT[Dynatrace]
    E --> C[Console]
Part Job In this lab Receiver Gets data in file_log reads a file Processor Changes data on the way (filter, mask, batch) Next lab Exporter Sends data out otlp_http to Dynatrace, debug to the console Pipeline Connects them in the service: section One logs pipeline

A component that is defined but not listed in a pipeline does nothing.

docs.title: Which collector image?
docs.text:
Component Dynatrace distro 0.58.0 Upstream contrib 0.162.0 file_log receiver yes yes otlp receiver yes yes host_metrics receiver yes yes prometheus receiver yes yes filter processor yes yes transform processor yes yes redaction processor yes yes log_dedup processor no yes otlp_http exporter yes yes debug exporter yes yes opamp extension no yes Image size on disk 220 MB 482 MB Image size compressed 45 MB 103 MB

The table comes from running components on both images. You can repeat it:

docker run --rm ghcr.io/dynatrace/dynatrace-otel-collector/dynatrace-otel-collector:0.58.0 components

To see the sizes on your machine, pull the images and list them:

docker images | grep -E "dynatrace-otel-collector|opentelemetry-collector-contrib"

DISK USAGE is the unpacked size on your machine. CONTENT SIZE is the compressed size, close to what you download from a registry.

Both images are big, because they contain many components you will never use. Can we ship only the parts we need? Yes. In Lab 07 you build your own collector that is a fraction of this size.

This lab uses the Dynatrace distro, because it has every component we need and it is smaller. Lab 06 uses contrib, because it needs log_dedup.

Component names

In these versions, component names use an underscore: file_log, otlp_http, log_dedup. Older guides write filelog, otlphttp, logdedup. If you copy a config from the internet, check the names.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
The lab files are in labs/05-collector-basics/. Docker must be running. You also run one Python script, so turn on the virtual environment from Setup in your second terminal.

  1. Go to the lab folder. It contains an empty live.log, the file the collector will read: 
    cd labs/05-collector-basics
  2. Look at collector.yaml. It has one receiver, two exporters and one pipeline: 
    receivers:
  file_log:
    include: [/logs/live.log]
    start_at: beginning
exporters:
  otlp_http/dynatrace:
    endpoint: ${env:DT_ENDPOINT}/api/v2/otlp
    headers:
      Authorization: "Api-Token ${env:DT_API_TOKEN}"
  debug:
    verbosity: basic
service:
  pipelines:
    logs:
      receivers: [file_log]
      exporters: [otlp_http/dynatrace, debug]
  3. ${env:NAME} reads an environment variable. Your token stays out of the file.
  4. The collector adds /v1/logs to the endpoint by itself.
  5. otlp_http/dynatrace is a named instance: type/name. You can have many exporters of the same type.
  6. Check that the config is valid. This is the same check you would run in a build pipeline: 
    docker compose run --rm -e DT_ENDPOINT=https://example.live.dynatrace.com -e DT_API_TOKEN=x collector validate --config=/etc/otelcol/collector.yaml
    No output means the config is valid.

  7. Start the collector: 

    docker compose --env-file ../../.env up

    No Dynatrace tenant? Print the logs in the console 

    docker compose -f docker-compose.yaml -f docker-compose.console.yaml up
    This uses collector.console.yaml: the same pipeline without the Dynatrace exporter. The debug exporter prints every log line in full.

  8. Open a second terminal, go to the same folder, and start a program that writes one log line per second. It repeats the lines of sample.log: 

    python append_logs.py

  9. Watch the first terminal. Each log records: 1 line is one log line that was read and exported.
  10. Open Dynatrace, open the Logs app, and filter with content = *"order-service"*. Your lines appear after a few seconds.

Stop the program with Ctrl+C. Stop the collector with Ctrl+C, then clean up:

docker compose down

Then empty live.log again, so you can repeat the lab with a clean file: git restore live.log.

docs.title: Expected result
docs.text:
In the collector terminal:

info  Logs  {"otelcol.component.id": "debug", "otelcol.signal": "logs", "log records": 1}

In Dynatrace, log lines like these:

INFO order-service GET /api/orders/48214 status=200 duration_ms=142
WARN payment-service Connection reset by peer while calling downstream billing-api
INFO account-service password reset for uid=jsmith email=john.smith999@gmail.com

Look at that last line

It contains an email address. The collector sent it to Dynatrace without a question. The next lab fixes this.

Screenshot placeholder: the Dynatrace Logs app with the order-service lines.

docs.title: Other receivers
docs.text:
The file is one way to get data in. A few more that the Dynatrace distro includes:

Receiver Gets Use it for otlp Traces, metrics, logs from apps Your instrumented apps (next exercise) host_metrics CPU, memory, disk, network Machine health prometheus Metrics from /metrics endpoints Apps that already expose Prometheus metrics

These are only a few. There are many more receivers for all kinds of cloud platforms and technologies (databases, message queues, Kubernetes, AWS, Azure, GCP and more). Browse the full list in the OpenTelemetry Collector contrib repository.

docs.title: Exercise: send the Lab 03 app through the collector
docs.text:
Now the collector also receives OTLP. We add an otlp receiver and a pipeline for each signal (collector.otlp.yaml).

  1. Stop the collector from the steps above: 
    docker compose down
  2. Start it again with the extra config. It publishes port 4318 (OTLP over HTTP) to your machine: 
    docker compose --env-file ../../.env -f docker-compose.yaml -f docker-compose.otlp.yaml up
  3. In a second terminal, start Lab 03 and point it at the collector instead of Dynatrace. The file docker-compose.collector.yaml only changes the endpoint: 
    cd ../03-manual-instrumentation
docker compose --env-file ../../.env -f docker-compose.yaml -f docker-compose.collector.yaml up --build
    The apps run in containers. They reach the collector on your machine at host.docker.internal.

  4. Send an order:

    macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
    curl "localhost:9000/order/1?quantity=2"

    Type curl.exe. In PowerShell, plain curl is a different command.

    curl.exe "localhost:9000/order/1?quantity=2"

  5. In the collector terminal, you see traces, metrics and logs. In Dynatrace, you see the same trace as in Lab 03.

The app did not change. Only one environment variable changed: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT. Now you can filter, mask or route this data in one place.

docs.title: Stuck?
docs.text:
• unsupported protocol scheme "" in the collector output: you forgot --env-file ../../.env, or .env is empty.
  • 401 or 403 in the collector output: the token has no logs.ingest scope. See Setup.
  • 404 from Dynatrace: the endpoint must be the base URL, like https://abc12345.live.dynatrace.com. No /api/v2/otlp and no trailing slash in .env. The config adds the path.
  • No log lines in the collector: check that append_logs.py runs in the lab folder, and that live.log exists before you start the collector (if you deleted it, run git restore live.log; Docker would otherwise create a folder with that name). On Linux, check the file permissions.
  • unknown type: "filelog": the name is file_log in this version.
  • Lab 03 cannot reach the collector (Linux): the override file adds host.docker.internal for you. Check that the collector container is running and port 4318 is free.
  • Port 4318 is in use: another collector or app uses it. Stop it.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Add the host_metrics receiver and a metrics pipeline. What do you see?
  • Change verbosity: basic to detailed in the debug exporter. What attributes does the file_log receiver add?
  • Add the batch processor to the pipeline. Many production collectors use it. What does it do, and what trade-offs does it bring?

docs.title: Lab 06: Processors
docs.text: Time: 25 minutes

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Add processors to the collector from Lab 05. Drop log lines you do not need, hide an email address, and collapse repeated lines. Measure how much data you save.

Let's reduce log volume by 64%

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Many backends charge by volume, and some log lines add little value: health checks, debug output, the same error 1000 times. Logs can also hold personal data that must not leave your network. A processor fixes this before the data leaves the collector. The app does not change.

docs.title: The logs
docs.text:
sample.log (in labs/06-processors, which you open in the steps below) has 11 lines. Read them and find the problems:

INFO order-service GET /api/orders/48214 status=200 duration_ms=142
INFO order-service GET /health status=200 duration_ms=3                 <- health check
INFO order-service GET /health status=200 duration_ms=1                 <- health check
WARN payment-service Connection reset by peer while calling downstream billing-api   <- repeated
WARN payment-service Connection reset by peer while calling downstream billing-api   <- repeated
WARN payment-service Connection reset by peer while calling downstream billing-api   <- repeated
DEBUG order-service Cache lookup for key=order:48214 result=miss        <- debug noise
INFO account-service password reset for uid=jsmith email=john.smith999@gmail.com     <- personal data
INFO payment-service Payment for txn tCode=PYMT-7784-AU amount=129.50 currency=AUD status=200
INFO order-service GET /api/orders/48214 status=500
INFO order-service GET /health status=200 duration_ms=2                 <- health check

docs.title: The tools
docs.text:
Processor What it does Use it when filter Drops records that match a rule The whole record has no value transform Changes a record (here: replace text) The record is useful, but one part is not log_dedup Collapses identical records into one with a count The same message repeats

Which image?

This lab uses the contrib image (0.162.0). The Dynatrace distro has filter, transform and redaction, but not log_dedup. See the table in Lab 05. Contrib is bigger, so Lab 07 shows how to build your own.

The rules are written in OTTL, the OpenTelemetry Transformation Language. IsMatch(log.body, "...") is true when the log text matches a regular expression. A filter condition says what to drop.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
The lab files are in labs/06-processors/. Docker must be running. You also run a Python script to measure the result, so turn on the virtual environment from Setup in your terminal.

  1. Go to the lab folder: 
    cd labs/06-processors
  2. Open collector.yaml. It defines five processors, but the pipeline uses none: 
    service:
  pipelines:
    logs:
      receivers: [file_log]
      processors: []
      exporters: [otlp_http/dynatrace, debug]
    The collector reads sample.log once, from the start. The debug exporter prints every record in full, so we can count them.
  3. Start it with no processors. This is our baseline: 
    docker compose --env-file ../../.env up -d
No Dynatrace tenant? 

docker compose up -d
The Dynatrace exporter will print errors. Ignore them. The debug output is correct. Use --force-recreate and docker compose down as in the steps below, without --env-file.

  1. Wait 15 seconds. Then measure: 
    docker compose logs collector --no-log-prefix | python measure_reduction.py sample.log
    The script counts the lines in sample.log and the records the collector exported. You should see 11 records, 0% reduction, and Email visible: YES (leak!).
  2. Stop the collector. Do this before every change: 
    docker compose down

You will now add each processor one by one and measure the reduction in log volume. The reduction percentage will increase each time we add a new processor.

docs.title: Exercise 1: Filter out health pings
docs.text:
Edit the processors: list in collector.yaml. Change:

processors: []

to:

processors: [filter/health]

Then run:

docker compose --env-file ../../.env up -d --force-recreate

Now run the measure command:

docker compose logs collector --no-log-prefix | python measure_reduction.py sample.log

You should see the logs have dropped from 11 to 8 (a 27% reduction) and the /health pings are no longer visible.

and run

docker compose down

docs.title: Exercise 2: Also filter out DEBUG logs
docs.text:
Edit processors in collector.yaml again and change:

processors: [filter/health]

to:

processors: [filter/health, filter/low_value]
Then run:

docker compose --env-file ../../.env up -d --force-recreate

Wait 15 seconds, run the measure command:

docker compose logs collector --no-log-prefix | python measure_reduction.py sample.log

You should see 11 logs have now been reduced to 7 (a 36% reduction) and the DEBUG lines are no longer present in the collector output.

docs.title: Exercise 3: Also deduplicate identical logs
docs.text:
Edit processors in collector.yaml again and change:

processors: [filter/health, filter/low_value]

to:

processors: [filter/health, filter/low_value, log_dedup]
Then run:

docker compose --env-file ../../.env up -d --force-recreate

Run the measure command:

docker compose logs collector --no-log-prefix | python measure_reduction.py sample.log

You should see 11 logs have now been reduced to 5 (a 55% reduction).

docs.title: Exercise 4: Also drop the line with personal data
docs.text:
Edit processors in collector.yaml again and change:

processors: [filter/health, filter/low_value, log_dedup]

to:

processors: [filter/health, filter/low_value, log_dedup, filter/personal_info]
Then run:

docker compose --env-file ../../.env up -d --force-recreate

Wait 15 seconds, run the measure command:

docker compose logs collector --no-log-prefix | python measure_reduction.py sample.log

You should see 11 logs have now been reduced to 4 (a 64% reduction) and Email visible: no. The whole password reset line is gone.

Run:

docker compose down

docs.title: Exercise 5: Mask the email instead of dropping the line
docs.text:
Dropping the line also hides the fact that a password reset happened. Edit processors in collector.yaml again and change:

processors: [filter/health, filter/low_value, log_dedup, filter/personal_info]

to:

processors: [filter/health, filter/low_value, log_dedup, transform/mask_email]
Then run:

docker compose --env-file ../../.env up -d --force-recreate

Wait 15 seconds, run the measure command:

docker compose logs collector --no-log-prefix | python measure_reduction.py sample.log

You should see 11 logs have now been reduced to 5 (a 55% reduction). The measure script reports Email visible: no. The password reset line is still there. To see the masked text in the collector's debug output, run:

macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
docker compose logs collector --no-log-prefix | grep "password reset"

docker compose logs collector --no-log-prefix | Select-String "password reset"

You should see email=***@*** in the line.

Run:

docker compose down

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Stage processors: list What it does 1 [filter/health] Drops the 3 health checks 2 [filter/health, filter/low_value] Also drops the DEBUG line 3 [filter/health, filter/low_value, log_dedup] Collapses 3 identical warnings into 1 4 [filter/health, filter/low_value, log_dedup, filter/personal_info] Drops the line that has an email 5 [filter/health, filter/low_value, log_dedup, transform/mask_email] Masks the email, keeps the line

Stages 4 and 5 are two answers to the same problem. Exercise 5 replaces the filter from Exercise 4 with a mask.

Why does log_dedup wait 10 seconds?

log_dedup holds records for a time window (interval: 10s) and counts the identical ones. At the end of the window it sends one record with an attribute log_duplicates: 3. This is why we wait before we measure. It is also why log_dedup goes after the first two filters: there is no reason to count records you will drop.

docs.title: Drop or mask?
docs.text:
filter (drop) transform (mask) Result The line is gone The line stays, one part changes Volume Lower Almost the same You still see Nothing That a password reset happened, for which user Risk You lose useful events A bad pattern can miss some data Pick it when The line has no value The line has value, but part of it is sensitive

Our line says "password reset for uid=jsmith". That event is useful for security. Dropping it hides it. Masking is the better choice here. The solution uses masking.

Masking is not perfect

The mask only catches what the pattern matches. The line still has uid=jsmith. Think about what else is personal data in your own logs. Test your patterns with real samples.

docs.title: Expected result
docs.text:
Run the finished config (stage 5) to check:

docker compose --env-file ../../.env -f docker-compose.yaml -f docker-compose.solution.yaml up -d --force-recreate
sleep 15
docker compose logs collector --no-log-prefix | python measure_reduction.py sample.log
docker compose down

We measured these numbers with the pinned versions:

Stage Records Reduction 0. No processors 11 0% 1. filter/health 8 27% 2. + filter/low_value 7 36% 3. + log_dedup 5 55% 4. + drop the email line 4 64% 5. + mask the email (instead of drop) 5 55%

The debug output (docker compose logs collector --no-log-prefix, before docker compose down) shows the masked email and the count:

Body: Str(INFO account-service password reset for uid=jsmith email=***@***)
Body: Str(WARN payment-service Connection reset by peer while calling downstream billing-api)
     -> log_duplicates: Int(3)

About the 63% number

Other material says "reduce by 63%". That is 7 of 11 lines removed (63.6%). Our script counts 4 of 11 records left with stage 4, and rounds the reduction to 64%. The number is measured, not assumed. With masking (stage 5) one more line stays, so the saving is 55%.

Screenshot placeholder: the Dynatrace Logs app after stage 5. 5 records, one with log_duplicates=3, and no email.

In Dynatrace, search for order-service again. The email line shows email=***@***, and no /health lines arrive.

docs.title: Stuck?
docs.text:
• unsupported protocol scheme "" errors: DT_ENDPOINT is empty. Use --env-file ../../.env. Your records are still counted correctly.
  • The count is lower than expected (for example 3): the collector did not wait for log_dedup. Wait 15 seconds, then measure.
  • The count is the same as before: you did not use --force-recreate, so the old config is still running. Reset and start again: 
    docker compose down
docker compose up -d
  • 'processors' ... unknown type: check that you spelled the name as in the processors: section, like filter/health.
  • YAML errors: indentation is part of YAML. Use spaces, not tabs. The config in some older material has wrong indentation (log_record must be under logs, which is under the processor name).
  • The email is still visible: you ran stage 1, 2 or 3 only. Add stage 4 or 5.
  • Validate before you run: 
    docker compose run --rm collector validate --config=/etc/otelcol/collector.yaml

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Use redaction instead of transform. It is built to hide secrets in attributes. Parse the log text into attributes first, then redact them.
  • Add a processor that drops all INFO lines unless they have status=500.
  • See more patterns in dynatrace/demo-opentelemetry-patterns.

docs.title: Lab 07: Custom collector with OCB
docs.text: Time: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Build your own collector that contains only the components you need. Run the Lab 06 pipeline on it and compare the image size with the contrib image.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
The contrib image has hundreds of components. You use a handful, but you ship and patch all of them. A smaller collector starts faster, has a smaller attack surface, and is easier to review. It is also the only way to use a component that no ready-made image includes.

The tool for this is the OpenTelemetry Collector Builder, called OCB (ocb). You give it a list of components. It generates Go code and compiles one binary.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
The lab files are in labs/07-ocb/. Docker must be running. You do not need Go: the build runs inside Docker. You also run a Python script to measure the result, so turn on the virtual environment from Setup.

  1. Go to the lab folder: 
    cd labs/07-ocb
  2. Open builder-config.yaml. This is the manifest. It lists every component. Each gomod line is a Go module and a version: 
    processors:
  - gomod: github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/processor/filterprocessor v0.162.0
  - gomod: github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/processor/logdedupprocessor v0.162.0
    It has the two receivers, two processors and two exporters that Lab 06 needs. Nothing else.
  3. Open Dockerfile. It has two stages. The first runs ocb to compile the collector. The second copies only the binary into a tiny image.
  4. Build it. This downloads and compiles Go code, so it takes 2-3 minutes: 
    docker compose build
  5. List the components inside your new collector: 
    docker run --rm otelcol-masterclass:0.162.0 components
    You should see file_log and otlp, then filter and log_dedup, then debug and otlp_http. Nothing more.

  6. Compare the size with the contrib image from Lab 06: 

    docker images | grep -E "otelcol-masterclass|opentelemetry-collector-contrib"
    There are two size columns:

    • DISK USAGE is the unpacked size on your machine. This is the number we compare.
    • CONTENT SIZE is the compressed size, close to what you download from a registry.

Your collector is much smaller in both. 7. Run the Lab 06 pipeline on your collector. collector.yaml here is the Lab 06 solution. 

docker compose --env-file ../../.env up -d

No Dynatrace tenant? 

docker compose up -d
The Dynatrace exporter will print errors. Ignore them.

  1. Wait 15 seconds. Then measure: 
    docker compose logs collector --no-log-prefix | python measure_reduction.py sample.log
  2. Clean up: 
    docker compose down

docs.title: Expected result
docs.text:
• The components list has exactly the 6 components in the manifest.
  • Your image is about 62 MB on disk. The contrib image is about 482 MB.
  • The measure script shows 11 input lines, 4 records exported (a 64% reduction), and no email, /health or DEBUG lines. It is the same result as Lab 06, from a much smaller collector.

docs.title: Stuck?
docs.text: Problem Fix unknown type: "filelog" Component names use an underscore in this version: file_log. See Lab 05. unknown type for any component The component is not in builder-config.yaml. Add its gomod line and run docker compose build again. Build fails with a network error The build downloads Go modules. Check your connection or proxy and try again. Version mismatch error Keep the v0.162.0 version the same on every line, and the same as dist.version.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Add the host_metrics receiver. Find its gomod line on opentelemetry.io/ecosystem/registry, add it to the manifest, rebuild, and check it with components.
  • Run the builder with --skip-compilation to see the generated Go code.

docs.title: Lab 08: Semantic conventions
docs.text: Time: 15 minutes (discussion and exercise)

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Find out for yourself why shared attribute names matter. Write one log line, compare it with the rest of the room, then run one query across messy and standard logs.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Your company has many teams, and every team writes telemetry. Does it all look the same? Let's find out.

Do the exercise first

Do not read past Part 1 until you have finished it. Later parts reveal the point of the exercise.

docs.title: Part 1: Exercise (5 minutes)
docs.text:
On paper or in a text editor, write one log line for a web server that handled a request. Use the format you normally use at work. Include:

  • the HTTP method
  • the status that was returned
  • the path that was requested
  • who the client was (IP address)

Now compare with the person next to you. Did you use the same order? The same words? The same format?

Keep your line. You need it in a minute.

docs.title: Part 2: Discuss (5 minutes)
docs.text:
Look at the lines in the room. Different order, different words, different formats. Now imagine one question for all of them: "show me all server errors". You need one query for each team. Dashboards, alerts and AI tools all break the same way.

Semantic conventions are the fix. They are a list of standard names and meanings for common things, such as an HTTP request. They are part of OpenTelemetry. If everyone uses the same name, one query works for everyone.

OpenTelemetry already has conventions for HTTP, databases, messaging, cloud, Kubernetes, GenAI and more. Here are the four we use in this section:

Meaning Standard name Example HTTP method http.request.method GET HTTP status code http.response.status_code 500 URL path url.path /api/orders Client IP address client.address 10.0.0.5

You have already used them. In Lab 01, the auto instrumentation set http.request.method and http.response.status_code on the spans for you. That is why OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN: http is in the Docker Compose files: it selects the new, stable HTTP names.

Browse the full list: opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv.

What is in a convention?

A convention is not only a name. It also says the type (string, number), the meaning, example values, and how stable it is (stable or development).

Rewrite your own line from Part 1 with these four names. How different is it from what you wrote?

docs.title: Part 3: Try one query (5 minutes)
docs.text:
Now see the problem in a real backend. You send the same 7 requests to Dynatrace twice, once from the messy logs and once from the standardised logs. Then you ask one question of both with DQL (Dynatrace Query Language), using the dtctl command line tool.

You need Python 3.11+, a Dynatrace tenant and dtctl. See Setup. The token needs the logs.ingest scope. No tenant? Use the fallback at the end of this part.

  1. Go to the folder and turn on the virtual environment from Setup:

    macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
    cd labs/08-semantic-conventions
source ../../.venv/bin/activate

    cd labs\08-semantic-conventions
..\..\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

  2. Read messy.log. These are 7 logs from 7 "teams". All 7 are the same kind of event: a handled HTTP request. 

    GET /api/orders 200 from 10.0.0.5
[checkout] method=POST path=/pay status_code=500 client=10.0.0.9
2026-10-16 INFO order-svc: user at 10.0.0.7 requested GET /api/orders/42 -> HTTP 404
{"verb":"GET","uri":"/health","code":200,"ip":"10.0.0.5"}
inventory: 10.0.0.8 "PUT /stock/7" 503
{"verb":"POST","uri":"/pay","code":502,"ip":"10.0.0.9"}
payment-svc: http.request.method=POST url.path=/refund http.response.status_code=200 client.address=10.0.0.9
    Three of them are server errors (500, 503, 502).

  3. Send both files to Dynatrace. messy.log is sent as plain text, one line per log record. standardised.log has the same 7 requests, but each name becomes an attribute. The script reads DT_ENDPOINT and DT_API_TOKEN from the .env file in the repo root: 
    python send_logs.py messy.log
python send_logs.py standardised.log
    You should see Sent 7 logs twice. Wait about 30 seconds for the logs to arrive.
  4. First check that the messy logs arrived. If dtctl says token ... not found, log in first: 
    dtctl auth login
    Then run the query: 
    dtctl query 'fetch logs
| filter service.name == "semconv-messy"
| fields timestamp, content'
    You should see all 7 lines, as plain text.
  5. Now ask for the server errors in the messy logs. The query uses the standard name http.response.status_code and a value of 500 or more. toLong turns the value into a number, because Dynatrace shows it as text: 
    dtctl query 'fetch logs
| filter service.name == "semconv-messy"
| filter toLong(http.response.status_code) >= 500'
    You should get no records (No resources found.). The 7 logs are there, and 3 of them are real errors, but the query finds none.
  6. Run the same query on the standardised logs. Only the service.name is different: 
    dtctl query 'fetch logs
| filter service.name == "semconv-standardised"
| filter toLong(http.response.status_code) >= 500
| fields timestamp, content, http.request.method, url.path, http.response.status_code'
    You should get 3 records: the 500, the 502 and the 503.

The query did not change. Only the names did.

No Dynatrace tenant? Run the query on your laptop

count_errors.py runs the same rule on the files, with no network: 

python count_errors.py messy.log
python count_errors.py standardised.log
You should see Server errors found: 0, then Server errors found: 3.

docs.title: Expected result
docs.text:
Data Server errors found Real server errors semconv-messy 0 3 semconv-standardised 3 3

To make the first one work, you would need a different rule for every team, and a new rule every time a new team starts. That does not scale.

docs.title: Stuck?
docs.text:
• python: command not found: the virtual environment is not on. See Setup.
  • The standardised query finds nothing: the logs can take a minute to arrive. Check the time range, and that the token has logs.ingest. Check that toLong(...) is in the query: without it, text is compared to a number and nothing matches.
  • You get 6 or 9 records, not 3: you ran send_logs.py more than once. Each run adds the same logs again. Add from:-10m after fetch logs to see only the latest.
  • send_logs.py fails with KeyError: 'DT_ENDPOINT': the script found no .env file, or it has no DT_ENDPOINT. Check .env in the repo root. See Setup.
  • The messy query returns records: you changed messy.log, or you sent a file twice with a different name.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Look at your own logs. Which standard names could you use? Search the attribute registry.
  • You do not have a convention for something, for example a cost code or a team name? You can write your own. But how do you make sure everyone uses it correctly? Next: Lab 09: Weaver.

docs.title: Lab 09: Weaver
docs.text: Time: 25 minutes

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Invent a custom attribute that OpenTelemetry does not have, write it down as a machine-readable convention, then use Weaver to check live telemetry against it. You will see what a good, a bad and a wrong record look like.

docs.title: The scenario
docs.text:
Imagine you work for ACME Corporation. ACME runs a shared observability platform, and many teams send their telemetry to it. That platform costs money, and Finance wants to charge each team for what it sends.

To do that, Finance must answer one question: which team sent this telemetry?

Do the exercise first

Think about it for a few minutes before reading on. The rest of the lab reveals one possible answer.

docs.title: Part 1: Exercise (5 minutes)
docs.text:
Look at the OpenTelemetry attribute registry. Is there a standard attribute for "the internal cost code of the team that owns this service"? There is not. It is specific to ACME, so the OpenTelemetry project will never define it.

So you have to invent one. On paper or in a text editor, decide:

  1. The name. Something like cost.code or acme.cost.code. Which is better, and why?
  2. The format. What does a valid value look like? Free text? A number? A fixed pattern?
  3. Which signals need it. Logs, traces, metrics, or all of them?
  4. Who enforces it. Finance cannot read every log. How do you know teams really send it, and send it correctly?

Compare with the person next to you.

docs.title: Part 2: Discuss (5 minutes)
docs.text:
Some things to think about:

  • Use a prefix you own. acme.cost.code is better than cost.code. OpenTelemetry may add its own cost.code one day with a different meaning, and your data would clash with it. The OpenTelemetry guidance is to put your own attributes in your own namespace, here acme..
  • The name is not enough. If one team sends acme.cost.code, another sends cost-code and a third sends acme.costcode, Finance cannot group anything. This is the same problem you saw in Lab 08.
  • The value must be valid. abc-12 or Marketing is useless for charging. We need a rule for the format.
  • A wiki page does not work. Nobody reads it, and nobody checks it.

We will use these decisions in this lab: the name is acme.cost.code, and the format is three capital letters and four digits, for example ABC1234. Every log record must have it.

docs.title: Why Weaver
docs.text:
Weaver is an OpenTelemetry tool that turns your convention into a schema (a registry) that a machine can read. With one schema you can:

  • check that telemetry follows the rules (we do this in this lab)
  • generate documentation and code
  • run the check in a CI/CD pipeline, so bad telemetry never reaches production
flowchart LR
    Reg["Registry<br/>(one definition)"] --> Check["Check live telemetry"]
    Reg --> Gen["Generate code and docs"]
    Check --> CI["CI/CD"]

docs.title: Part 3: Define it and check it
The files
docs.text:
The lab files are in labs/09-weaver/.

File What it does model/manifest.yaml Names our registry (acme). It also imports the standard OpenTelemetry conventions, so we check against both. model/imports.yaml Says "import everything" from the OpenTelemetry registry. model/cost.yaml Defines the new attribute acme.cost.code with a description and examples. policies/cost_code.rego Two rules: the value must match ^[A-Z]{3}[0-9]{4}$, and every log must have the attribute. emit_test_logs.py Sends 3 test logs to Weaver.

The registry and the policy do different jobs

cost.yaml says the key exists and what it means. The descriptions and examples are for humans. The format of the value is checked by the policy in cost_code.rego (written in a language called Rego). Weaver does not read the regex from the YAML.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
Docker must be running. You need Python 3.11+.

  1. Go to the lab folder and pull the Weaver image. The Weaver commands are defined in docker-compose.yaml, so they are the same on every OS: 
    cd labs/09-weaver
docker compose pull
  2. Check that the registry is valid: 
    docker compose run --rm check
    You should see ✔ No after_resolution policy violation. Weaver downloads the OpenTelemetry conventions the first time, so this can take a few seconds.
  3. Open two terminals in labs/09-weaver. In terminal 1, start Weaver in live-check mode. It is a server that waits for telemetry on port 4317 and checks every record. It stops after 30 seconds without data: 
    docker compose run --rm --service-ports live-check
    Wait until you see OTLP gRPC listener started.

  4. In terminal 2, go to the lab folder, activate the environment and send the 3 test logs:

    macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
    source ../../.venv/bin/activate
python emit_test_logs.py

    ..\..\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
