python emit_test_logs.py

  5. Go back to terminal 1. Wait for Weaver to stop, or press Ctrl+C. It prints a report.

docs.title: Expected result
docs.text:
Weaver prints one block per log. Read the Log part of each block. Colours in the terminal: green is fine, red is a violation.

Log 1: good is compliant. Every attribute is green.

Log
    acme.cost.code = ABC1234

Log 2: bad-format has the right key, but a wrong value:

Log
    acme.cost.code = abc-12
        - [violation] acme.cost.code value 'abc-12' does not match ^[A-Z]{3}[0-9]{4}$

Log 3: wrong-key has the right value, but the wrong key. Two violations: the key is not in the registry, and the required key is missing:

Log
    - [violation] Log record is missing required attribute 'acme.cost.code'
    cost-code = ABC1234
        - [violation] Attribute 'cost-code' does not exist in the registry.

At the end is a summary. We got 3 violations (one per bad log) and 3 improvement messages:

Advisories given
  - total: 6
  - advice level:
    - improvement: 3
    - violation: 3

What are the 3 improvements?

Each log also has service.instance.id, which the SDK adds. In this OpenTelemetry version it is not stable yet, so Weaver says so. It is only advice. You can ignore it.

Weaver has levels: violation (must fix), improvement (should fix) and information (FYI). You choose the level in your policy.

docs.title: Exercise: add an enum attribute
docs.text:
ACME also wants an attribute acme.environment. Only two values are allowed: prod and staging.

  1. Add this to the end of model/cost.yaml, under attributes: (keep the indentation: it lines up with - id: acme.cost.code): 
          - id: acme.environment
        type:
          members:
            - id: production
              value: prod
              stability: stable
            - id: staging
              value: staging
              stability: stable
        stability: stable
        brief: Environment the telemetry came from.
        examples: ["prod", "staging"]
  2. Check the registry again (step 2).
  3. In emit_test_logs.py, change the good and bad-format lines to: 
    "good": ("team-a", {"acme.cost.code": "ABC1234", "acme.environment": "prod"}),
"bad-format": ("team-b", {"acme.cost.code": "abc-12", "acme.environment": "production"}),
  4. Run Weaver (step 3), then send the logs (step 4).

You should see that acme.environment = prod is clean, and for production Weaver says:

acme.environment = production
    - [information] Enum attribute 'acme.environment' has value 'production' which is not documented.

An enum is checked by Weaver without a policy. You only had to define it. Notice the level is information, not violation. To make it a hard failure, you would write a Rego rule like the one in cost_code.rego.

docs.title: Weaver in a pipeline
docs.text: Weaver can write its report as JSON or YAML (--output), so a CI/CD job can read it. A team could run their tests with Weaver in live-check mode, and fail the build on any violation. See weaver registry live-check --help.

docs.title: Stuck?
docs.text:
• Cannot connect to the Docker daemon: start Docker.
  • port is already allocated (4317): a collector from another lab is running. Stop it from that lab's folder: 
    docker compose down
  • The Python script prints errors about the connection: Weaver is not ready yet. Wait for OTLP gRPC listener started, then run it again.
  • Weaver stops before you send logs: the 30 second timeout ran out. Start it again.
  • registry check fails with a YAML error: indentation. Use spaces, not tabs. The new attribute must line up with the first one.
  • No difference after you edit the registry: Weaver reads model/ when it starts. Stop it and start it again.
  • ModuleNotFoundError: opentelemetry: you did not activate the environment in terminal 2.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Add a Rego rule that makes an unknown acme.environment value a violation.
  • Point Weaver at a real app: send the OTLP data from Lab 03 to port 4317. Which of your custom attributes (order.id, shop.orders) are not in any registry?
  • Read the Weaver docs and the original hands-on repo. It also checks plain-text logs coming from a collector filelog receiver. Why do you think the plain-text log fails the check?

docs.title: Lab 10: OpAMP
docs.text: Time: 20 minutes

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Run a small OpAMP server, connect two collectors to it, then change the config of a running collector by editing one file on the server. You never touch the collector.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
One collector is easy to manage. A thousand are not. You need to answer: which collectors exist, are they healthy, and what config do they run? You also need to change that config without logging in to each machine.

OpAMP (Open Agent Management Protocol) is the standard for this. Each collector (the agent) connects to a server. The agent reports who it is, its health and its config. The server can send back new config.

flowchart LR
    S["OpAMP server<br/>(your laptop)"]
    S <-->|status and config| A1["plain collector"]
    S <-->|status and config| A2["Supervisor + collector"]

OpAMP messages use protobuf, a compact binary format. It is like JSON, but the bytes carry only field numbers, not names. A shared .proto file says what each number means. The folder labs/10-opamp/opamp/v1/ holds Python code generated from the OpAMP .proto files, so the server can read and write the messages. You do not need to run anything to make it.

docs.title: The scenario
docs.text: A collector tails a log file. As is normal in production, it drops DEBUG logs to save cost and noise. Then there is an incident, and you need the DEBUG detail now. You will edit a file on the server, and the DEBUG lines will start to flow. When the incident ends, you revert it.

docs.title: The files
docs.text:
The lab files are in labs/10-opamp/.

File What it does server.py The OpAMP server. It lists agents, watches remote-config.yaml and pushes it to agents. remote-config.yaml The file the server watches. Whatever is in it is what agents are told to run. examples/baseline.yaml Normal state: keep the local filter, so DEBUG is dropped. examples/capture-debug.yaml Incident state: remove the filter, so DEBUG is kept. docker-compose.yaml Two agents: plain and agent. agent/collector.yaml The collector's local config: tail logs/file.log, read the level, drop DEBUG, print the rest. agent/supervisor.yaml Tells the Supervisor where the server is and that it accepts remote config.

Why does the second agent need a Supervisor?

A collector's own opamp extension reports status, health and config. It cannot change the collector it lives in. That job belongs to the OpAMP Supervisor. It keeps the OpAMP connection, starts the collector as a child process, merges the remote config with the local config, and restarts the collector. So agent 2 is a Supervisor and a collector in one container.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text: Docker must be running. You need three terminals, all in the lab folder. The server runs on your machine and uses the Python environment from Setup.

docs.title: Part 1: Run the server and see an agent
docs.text:
1. Terminal 1. Start the server:

    macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
    cd labs/10-opamp
source ../../.venv/bin/activate
python server.py

    cd labs\10-opamp
..\..\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python server.py

    It prints * remote-config.yaml changed (...). It has read the file and is waiting for agents.

  2. Terminal 2. Start the plain collector: 

    cd labs/10-opamp
docker compose up -d plain

  3. Within a few seconds, terminal 1 prints + agent <id> connected. List what the server knows:

    macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
    curl -s localhost:4320/agents | python -m json.tool

    Type curl.exe. In PowerShell, plain curl is a different command.

    curl.exe -s localhost:4320/agents | python -m json.tool

    You see the agent's description (name, version, host), its health, and its capabilities. The capabilities are sent as one number (a bitmask, one bit per yes/no ability). The server turns it into names.

    Look at the list. There is no AcceptsRemoteConfig. This agent can report, but it cannot be told what to do.

docs.title: Part 2: Connect an agent that accepts config
docs.text:
1. Start the Supervisor agent (the first build takes about a minute): 
    docker compose up -d --build agent

  2. Terminal 1 shows the server sending the file and the agent applying it: 

    + agent 01a1438afaae7bac9c2097c7ac1990f9 connected
> agent 01a1438afaae7bac9c2097c7ac1990f9: sending remote-config.yaml
~ agent 01a1438afaae7bac9c2097c7ac1990f9 remote config APPLIED
    You see this once at start, even though the config equals the local one. The server sends the file to any agent that accepts it, as soon as it connects. Run the curl command again. Now there are two agents, and only one has AcceptsRemoteConfig and remote_config_status: APPLIED.

  3. Terminal 3. Watch what the collector prints, as just LEVEL message:

    macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
    cd labs/10-opamp
source ../../.venv/bin/activate
docker compose logs -f --no-log-prefix agent | python watch_collector.py

    cd labs\10-opamp
..\..\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
docker compose logs -f --no-log-prefix agent | python watch_collector.py

    The three DEBUG lines already in the log file are dropped, so you see nothing yet. That is the production baseline.

docs.title: Part 3: The incident
docs.text:
1. In terminal 2, write two log lines. One is INFO, one is DEBUG: 

    python lab.py log "INFO user logged in"
python lab.py log "DEBUG cache miss"
    lab.py is a small helper in the lab folder. It appends a line to logs/file.log. It works the same on every OS. Activate the environment in this terminal first, as in terminal 1. Terminal 3 shows only INFO user logged in. The DEBUG line is dropped.

  2. Incident! Turn on DEBUG capture. Open examples/capture-debug.yaml. It removes the filter from the logs pipeline: 

    service:
 pipelines:
   logs:
     processors: []
    Lists are replaced when configs merge, so an empty list removes the local filter/drop_debug. Copy it over the watched file: 
    python lab.py config capture-debug
    This copies examples/capture-debug.yaml over remote-config.yaml. You can also paste the file into remote-config.yaml in your editor and save.

  3. Terminal 1 shows the full round trip: 

    * remote-config.yaml changed (3ddcc841)
> agent 01a1438a...: pushed remote-config.yaml
~ agent 01a1438a... remote config APPLYING
~ agent 01a1438a... remote config APPLIED

  4. Write more logs: 

    python lab.py log "INFO payment failed"
python lab.py log "DEBUG retrying gateway call"
    This time terminal 3 shows both lines.

  5. Ask the server what the collector is really running. Use the instance_uid of the agent with APPLIED:

    macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
    curl -s localhost:4320/agents/<instance_uid>/effective-config

    Type curl.exe. In PowerShell, plain curl is a different command.

    curl.exe -s localhost:4320/agents/<instance_uid>/effective-config

    The logs pipeline now has no filter/drop_debug.

  6. Incident over. Revert: 

    python lab.py config baseline
python lab.py log "DEBUG should be dropped again"
    The DEBUG line no longer appears in terminal 3.

  7. Clean up. Press Ctrl-C in terminal 1 and in terminal 3, then run: 

    docker compose down
python lab.py reset
    reset puts remote-config.yaml and logs/file.log back to how they started.

docs.title: Expected result
docs.text:
• The plain collector shows up in /agents but cannot take config.
  • The Supervisor agent shows up with AcceptsRemoteConfig, and reports APPLYING then APPLIED each time you change remote-config.yaml.
  • DEBUG lines appear only while capture-debug.yaml is in place.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Two transports. OpAMP works over plain HTTP and over WebSocket. The plain collector uses HTTP. The agent polls, about every 30 seconds, and the server can only answer. The Supervisor uses a WebSocket, a long-lived connection where either side can send at any time. That is why the push in step 8 lands in about a second.
  • A hash for each config. The server sends the file with a SHA-256 hash of its contents. The agent sends the hash back when it has applied it. So the server knows what each agent runs, and does not resend it.
  • Sequence numbers. Every agent message has a number that goes up by 1. If the server sees a gap (for example, after the server restarted and lost its memory), it sets the ReportFullState flag, and the agent resends everything about itself.
  • The registry lives in memory. Restart the server and it forgets all agents until they reconnect. A real server stores this in a database.

docs.title: Stuck?
docs.text:
• No agent connects: the containers reach your machine as host.docker.internal. This works on Docker Desktop and Rancher Desktop. On Linux, add this to both services in docker-compose.yaml: 
    extra_hosts:
  - "host.docker.internal:host-gateway"
    Do not add it on macOS or Windows. It points to the wrong address there.
  • Failed to connect to the OpAMP server in the agent log: the server is not running, or you started the agent before the server. The agent retries. It connects once the server is up.
  • No supported WebSocket library detected: your environment is missing websockets. Run pip install -r requirements.txt from the repo root.
  • ModuleNotFoundError: google.protobuf or fastapi: activate the environment in this terminal (see Setup).
  • port is already allocated or address already in use (4320): an old server is still running. Stop it with Ctrl-C.
  • Nothing changes after you copy the file: the server checks the file once a second. Look for * remote-config.yaml changed in terminal 1. If it is missing, check you copied it over remote-config.yaml in labs/10-opamp.
  • Terminal 3 shows old or missing lines: the collector remembers how far it has read the file (the file_storage extension), so it only prints new lines. If you ran the lab before, run docker compose down and run python lab.py reset.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Add a second Supervisor agent. Copy the agent service in docker-compose.yaml and give it its own logs folder. One file change now reconfigures both. This is the point of OpAMP.
  • Send a config that is broken (for example processors: [does-not-exist]). What status does the agent report? Does the collector keep working?
  • Read the OpAMP specification and the kcd-indonesia-2026 repo. It builds this server one step at a time, from printing raw bytes up to remote config.
  • This server is for learning. What would a real one also need? Think about authentication, TLS, storage and thousands of agents. Lab 11 shows a product built for this.

docs.title: Lab 11: Bindplane (discussion and demo)
docs.text: Time: 5 minutes. The facilitator shows it. There are no lab files to run.

docs.title: 1. Goal
docs.text: See what a finished, product-grade OpAMP control plane looks like, and compare it with the small server you built in Lab 10.

docs.title: 2. Why it matters
docs.text:
In Lab 10 you edited one file and a running collector changed. That is the core idea. A real fleet needs much more:

  • thousands of collectors, grouped by environment or region,
  • a screen to build config without hand-writing YAML,
  • safe delivery, so one bad change does not break every collector,
  • login, TLS and storage.

Bindplane is an OpenTelemetry-native control plane built for this. It is a product, not part of the OpenTelemetry project. This lab is here to show the idea at scale, not to tell you to buy it.

docs.title: 3. How it works
docs.text:
Bindplane uses the same protocol as Lab 10. Each collector connects to the Bindplane server over OpAMP (a WebSocket) and receives config from it.

flowchart LR
    B["Bindplane server"]
    B <-->|OpAMP| C1["Collector"]
    B <-->|OpAMP| C2["Collector"]
    B <-->|OpAMP| C3["Collector"]
    C1 -->|OTLP| D["Backend"]
    C2 -->|OTLP| D
    C3 -->|OTLP| D

Telemetry does not pass through the Bindplane server. Collectors send it straight to your backend. The server only manages them.

Bindplane has these main ideas (source):

Concept What it is Lab 10 equivalent Collector An OpenTelemetry collector connected over OpAMP. Bindplane ships its own build, the BDOT collector. You can also connect a custom collector (for example from Lab 07) with the OpAMP Supervisor. The plain and agent containers Configuration A versioned pipeline of sources, processors and destinations. Bindplane turns it into collector YAML. remote-config.yaml Rollout How a new version reaches collectors, step by step. Copying a file and hoping Edge Fleet A named group of collectors that share one configuration. Not in Lab 10 Gateway A group of collectors that receive data from edge collectors, process it in one place, and forward it. Not in Lab 10

docs.title: Rollouts
docs.text:
In Lab 10 your change hit every agent at once. Bindplane does not do that:

  • Standard rollout (all editions): the new version goes to 3 collectors first. Then more follow in growing batches. If any collector reports an error, the rollout pauses.
  • Progressive rollout (Enterprise only): you define stages by label, for example env=staging then env=production. It stops after each stage until you continue.

You can also roll back to an earlier version.

docs.title: 4. Demo (facilitator)
docs.text:
Show these four things in the Bindplane UI. Keep it to five minutes.

  1. The collector list. Point out that it is the same information as the agent list in Lab 10: who is connected, and their health.
  2. A configuration. Show sources, processors and destinations as blocks. Say: "This is the YAML from Lab 06, built with clicks."
  3. A change. Add or remove a processor, for example a filter that drops DEBUG logs. This repeats Lab 10 in the UI.
  4. The rollout. Start it. Show the staged delivery and the diff between the old and new version.

Facilitator

Check the demo works on your account before the session. Plans and features change, and Progressive rollouts need Enterprise.

docs.title: 5. Discussion questions
docs.text:
1. Lab 10's server forgot every agent when it restarted. What must a real server store?
  2. A rollout pauses when a collector reports an error. What could still go wrong that the collector would not report? (Think: valid config that drops the wrong data.)
  3. Telemetry skips the Bindplane server. What is the good side of that? What happens to your collectors if the server is down?
  4. You must choose between a vendor control plane and building on the OpAMP server in the OpenTelemetry repositories. What would you weigh? (Think: cost, support, lock-in, effort.)
  5. When would you add a Gateway tier instead of sending from every edge collector straight to the backend?

docs.title: 6. Going further
docs.text:
• Bindplane documentation
  • Connect collectors using the OpAMP Supervisor. It shows how to manage a custom collector from Lab 07.
  • BDOT collector on GitHub
  • OpAMP specification

docs.title: OpenTelemetry Masterclass
docs.text:
We are building a hands on OpenTelemetry masterclass lab. It will be 2-3hrs. Attendees will have their own laptops.

We must assume a mixed OpenTelemetry knowledge so we start at the basics, move quickly (this code will be open sourced after the session so attendees will have access to it to repeat afterwards).

I am most familiar with Python so we use Python as examples throughout unless there's a strong reason not to.

Doccumentation will be build into ./docs folder as mkdocs-material website, we'll use mkdocs gh-deploy to store in gh-pages (the repo is NOT yet configred - I'll do that when we're built).

Audience first language will not be English so keep vocab super simple.
